coverage: Lesson 1 et Weeks 2, 3 et 5 (la Week 4 – recrutement et éthique – n'a pas encore été fournie)

fr: **Risque caché** : ce n'est pas l'exécution lente, c'est **l'exécution confiante de la mauvaise idée**. Une équipe peut livrer à l'heure et dans le budget et échouer si le problème client n'a jamais été réel.
**Définition** : le Customer Development est une manière disciplinée de **transformer des hypothèses en preuves, et des preuves en décisions** (Assumption → Evidence → Decision).

**Origines** : réponse aux échecs répétés de startups ; **2005** les Four Steps (Blank) ; **2012** le manuel opérationnel (Blank & Dorf) ; aujourd'hui interviews, observation, expériences, journaux de preuves.

**Search vs Execution** : une startup **cherche** un modèle (incertitude forte, hypothèses provisoires, progrès = incertitude réduite) ; une entreprise établie **exécute** un modèle connu (processus répétables, progrès = livraison fiable).

**Piège du business plan** : il écrit les hypothèses comme des faits. Le Customer Development les réécrit en **affirmations testables** : « Nous croyons que [segment] vit [problème] dans [contexte], causant [conséquence]. Nous chercherons ce qui pourrait nous donner tort. »

**4 étapes** : 1 **Customer Discovery** (problème réel ?) → 2 **Customer Validation** (le modèle se répète ?) → 3 **Customer Creation** (la demande peut croître ?) → 4 **Company Building** (l'organisation passe à l'échelle ?). **Le cours se concentre sur l'étape 1.**

**Discovery répond à 4 questions** : **WHO** (quelles personnes partagent un contexte pertinent), **WHAT** (quel problème), **HOW NOW** (quelles alternatives/contournements), **HOW SURE** (quelles preuves soutiennent ou contredisent).
en: **Hidden risk**: not slow execution but **confident execution of the wrong idea**. A team can deliver on time and on budget and still fail if the customer problem was never real.
**Definition**: Customer Development is a disciplined way to **turn assumptions into evidence and evidence into decisions** (Assumption → Evidence → Decision).
**Origins**: response to repeated startup failure; **2005** the Four Steps (Blank); **2012** the operating manual (Blank & Dorf); today interviews, observation, experiments and evidence logs.

**Search vs Execution**: a startup **searches** for a model (high uncertainty, provisional assumptions, progress = reduced uncertainty); an established company **executes** a known model (repeatable processes, progress = reliable delivery).

**The planning trap**: a business plan writes assumptions as if they were facts. Discovery rewrites them as **testable claims**: “We believe [segment] experiences [problem] in [context], causing [consequence]. We will look for evidence that could prove us wrong.”

**4 stages**: 1 **Customer Discovery** (real problem?) → 2 **Customer Validation** (can the model repeat?) → 3 **Customer Creation** (can demand grow?) → 4 **Company Building** (can the organisation scale?). **This course concentrates on Stage 1.**

**Discovery answers 4 questions**: **WHO** (which people share a relevant context), **WHAT** (which problem), **HOW NOW** (alternatives/workarounds), **HOW SURE** (what evidence supports or challenges the claim).

title.fr: Boucle d'apprentissage, risques et différences avec l'étude de marché / la vente
title.en: The learning loop, risks, and how discovery differs from research and selling

fr: **Deux pistes en parallèle** : Product (Concept, Design, Build, Launch, Scale) et Customer (Assumptions, Interviews, Patterns, Decision, Next test). **Un jalon produit n'est pas une preuve que l'hypothèse client est vraie.**

**Trois risques** : **Customer risk** (mauvais segment), **Problem risk** (problème faible, rare ou toléré), **Value risk** (trop petit pour pousser à agir). *Discovery achète de meilleures décisions, pas la certitude.*

**Dedans vs dehors** : à l'intérieur du bâtiment on a des opinions (croyances, débats de features, prévisions) ; à l'extérieur on observe des comportements (histoires récentes, contournements, coûts, arbitrages, contradictions).

**Boucle** : Assumption (rendre l'incertitude explicite) → Test (méthode + échantillon) → Evidence (comportement et contexte) → Decision (**continuer, resserrer, pivoter, arrêter**). Une boucle utile **se termine par une décision changée**, pas juste plus de notes.

**Discovery vs Market research vs Selling** : rôle principal = réduire l'incertitude / décrire un marché / créer une transaction ; preuves = histoires, comportements, alternatives / tendances, attitudes / objections, engagements ; posture = curieux et falsifiable / analytique / persuasif ; **mode d'échec** = pitcher l'idée / des moyennes qui cachent le contexte / prendre l'accord pour une preuve.
en: **Two parallel tracks**: Product (Concept, Design, Build, Launch, Scale) and Customer (Assumptions, Interviews, Patterns, Decision, Next test). **A product milestone is not evidence that the customer hypothesis is true.**

**Three risks**: **Customer risk** (wrong segment), **Problem risk** (weak, rare or tolerated problem), **Value risk** (too small to motivate action). *Discovery buys better decisions, not certainty.*
**Inside vs outside**: inside the building we have opinions (beliefs, feature debates, forecasts); outside we can observe behaviour (recent stories, workarounds, costs, trade-offs, contradictions).

**Loop**: Assumption (make uncertainty explicit) → Test (method + sample) → Evidence (behaviour and context) → Decision (**continue, narrow, pivot or stop**). A useful loop **ends with a changed decision**, not merely more notes.

**Discovery vs Market research vs Selling**: main job = reduce uncertainty / describe a market / create a transaction; evidence = stories, behaviour, alternatives / trends, attitudes / objections, commitments; stance = curious & falsifiable / analytical / persuasive; **failure mode** = pitching the idea / broad averages hide context / agreement mistaken for evidence.

fr: **5 termes** : **Assumption** = croyance traitée comme incertaine ; **Hypothesis** = affirmation spécifique et testable ; **Evidence** = observation pertinente pour l'affirmation ; **Insight** = interprétation qui explique un motif ; **Decision** = changement d'action justifié par les preuves.

**Observation ≠ interprétation ≠ claim** : « Elle a ouvert trois applis bancaires et copié les soldes dans Notes » = **observation** (directement vue) ; « elle essaie de créer une vue unique de son argent » = **interprétation** ; « les étudiants ont besoin d'un système de budget consolidé » = **claim** (généralisation testable). On écrit les trois mais on les **étiquette honnêtement**.

**Anatomie d'un problème (4 parties)** : **Segment** (qui), **Context** (quand/où), **Friction** (ce qui bloque), **Consequence** (coût, retard, risque, émotion). Si une partie est floue, l'hypothèse est difficile à tester et facile à confirmer.

**Unité d'analyse** : segment × contexte × problème × conséquence. Ex. : étudiants de 1re année × avant le loyer × ne voient pas leurs dépenses discrétionnaires × virements en retard et frais évitables.

**Problème vs solution** : « Je veux une app » est une **demande de solution**, pas une preuve. Demander l'histoire derrière : qu'est-il arrivé la dernière fois ? qu'as-tu fait ? qu'est-ce qui était difficile ? qu'est-ce que ça a coûté ?

**Hypothèse falsifiable** : « We believe [SEGMENT] in [CONTEXT] struggles with [PROBLEM] causing [CONSEQUENCE] » + « We would reconsider this if… ». Test : retirer tous les mots de solution, l'énoncé doit rester vrai.
en: **5 terms**: **Assumption** = a belief treated as uncertain; **Hypothesis** = a specific, testable claim; **Evidence** = an observation relevant to the claim; **Insight** = an interpretation that explains a pattern; **Decision** = a change in action justified by evidence.

**Observation ≠ interpretation ≠ claim**: “She opened three banking apps and copied balances into Notes” = **observation** (directly witnessed); “She is trying to create one view of her money” = **interpretation**; “Students need a consolidated budgeting system” = **claim** (testable generalisation). Write all three but **label them honestly**.

**Problem anatomy (4 parts)**: **Segment** (who), **Context** (when/where), **Friction** (what blocks progress), **Consequence** (cost, delay, risk, emotion). If one part is vague, the hypothesis is hard to test and easy to confirm.
**Unit of analysis**: segment × context × problem × consequence. E.g. first-year students × before rent is due × cannot see discretionary spending × late transfers and avoidable fees.
**Problem vs solution**: “I want an app” is a **solution request**, not evidence. Ask for the story behind it: what happened last time? what did you do? what was difficult? what did it cost?

**Falsifiable hypothesis**: “We believe [SEGMENT] in [CONTEXT] struggles with [PROBLEM] causing [CONSEQUENCE]” + “We would reconsider this if…”. Test: remove every solution word, the statement must still be true.

title.fr: Force de la preuve, alternatives, cas négatifs, éthique
title.en: Evidence strength, alternatives, negative cases, ethics

fr: **Échelle de preuve (5 = la plus forte)** : 5 comportement répété avec coût ou engagement réel · 4 histoire récente précise avec détails observables · 3 contournement/alternative actuelle · 2 attitude ou préférence générale · 1 intention future. *L'échelle classe la qualité, pas la certitude ; aucune interview ne prouve un marché.*

**Passé > intention** : éviter « Would you use…? / Would you pay…? / Do you like…? » (politesse, imagination, prédiction) ; préférer « Tell me about the last time… / What did you do next? / What did that cost? ».

**Alternatives et concurrence** : dedicated tool, general tool (tableur, chat, notes), manual workaround, delegation, **do nothing**. Si le client ne fait rien, demander ce qui rend le statu quo acceptable.

**Intensité du problème** = fréquence + conséquence + coût actuel. **Intensité ≠ volume de plaintes** : une plainte bruyante peut avoir peu de conséquences, un contournement silencieux peut coûter des heures chaque semaine.
**Cas négatifs** : les contradictions sont des données, elles protègent du biais de confirmation. Trois seaux : **Supports**, **Challenges**, **Unknown**.

**Preuve prête pour la décision** : **relevant, varied, traceable, ethical** (participation informée, minimisation des données, confidentialité, pas de pression trompeuse). Porte de décision : **Continue / Narrow / Pivot / Stop**. Ne pas appliquer une règle de taille d'échantillon mécaniquement.
en: **Evidence ladder (5 = strongest)**: 5 repeated behaviour with real cost or commitment · 4 recent specific story with observable detail · 3 current workaround or alternative · 2 general attitude or preference · 1 future intention. *The ladder ranks quality, not certainty; no single interview proves a market.*

**Past > intention**: avoid “Would you use…? / Would you pay…? / Do you like…?” (politeness, imagination, prediction); prefer “Tell me about the last time… / What did you do next? / What did that cost?”.

**Alternatives and competition**: dedicated tool, general tool (spreadsheet, chat, notes), manual workaround, delegation, **do nothing**. If the customer does nothing, ask what makes the status quo acceptable.
**Problem intensity** = frequency + consequence + current cost. **Intensity ≠ complaint volume**: a loud complaint may have little consequence; a quiet workaround may consume hours every week.
**Negative cases**: contradictions are data, they protect against confirmation bias. Three buckets: **Supports**, **Challenges**, **Unknown**.

**Decision-ready evidence**: **relevant, varied, traceable, ethical** (informed participation, data minimisation, confidentiality, no deceptive pressure). Decision gate: **Continue / Narrow / Pivot / Stop**. Don’t use a sample-size rule mechanically.

title.fr: Segmentation : de l'audience au segment de recherche
title.en: Segmentation: from audience to research segment

fr: **Audience vs segment** : l'audience cible est large (utile pour dimensionner le marché, souvent démographique) ; le **segment de recherche** est une situation pertinente, un comportement observable, des contraintes comparables, **filtrable avant l'interview**. *Un segment est une règle pour comparer des expériences, pas une description de marché.*

**4 lentilles** : **Context** (quand la tâche se produit ?) · **Behavior** (que se passe-t-il aujourd'hui ?) · **Constraint** (qu'est-ce qui bloque ou augmente le coût ?) · **Consequence** (qu'est-ce qui est perdu ?).

**Trop large vs cherchable** : « Freelancers de 20-45 ans » (trop large) vs « designers indépendants avec 3-8 clients actifs qui envoient eux-mêmes leurs factures et ont récemment relancé un paiement en retard » (cherchable).

**« Customer » = plusieurs rôles** : End user, Influencer, Recommender, Economic buyer (contrôle le budget), Decision maker (donne le oui final), **Saboteur** (protège le statu quo). Un même problème crée des douleurs différentes selon le rôle (exemple de la file d'attente en banque).

**Journée type** (day in the life) : repérer transitions, attentes, travail manuel, répétitions, tension émotionnelle. On en tire des **signaux comparables** (fréquence, qui initie, alternative actuelle, point d'attente, coût de l'erreur…).

**Échelle de douleur** : 1 a un problème · 2 le reconnaît · 3 cherche une solution · **4 a bricolé un contournement** · **5 a ou cherche un budget**. Les niveaux 4-5 sont utiles tôt car actions et coûts sont visibles.

**Criblage** : le **comportement bat l'étiquette**. Étiquettes faibles : aware, modern, busy, motivated. Signaux observables : a fait X le mois dernier, a payé une alternative, a construit un processus manuel, a retardé une autre tâche. Un critère qu'on ne peut pas vérifier neutralement est faible pour le recrutement.
en: **Audience vs segment**: the target audience is broad (useful for market sizing, often demographic); the **research segment** is one relevant situation, observable behaviour, comparable constraints, **screenable before the interview**. *A segment is a rule for comparing experience, not a market description.*
**4 lenses**: **Context** (when does the task occur?) · **Behavior** (what happens today?) · **Constraint** (what blocks or raises the cost?) · **Consequence** (what is lost?).

**Too broad vs researchable**: “Freelancers aged 20–45” (too broad) vs “self-employed designers with 3–8 active clients who send invoices themselves and recently chased a late payment” (researchable).

**“Customer” = several roles**: End user, Influencer, Recommender, Economic buyer (controls budget), Decision maker (gives the final yes), **Saboteur** (protects the status quo). The same situation creates different pain per role (bank queue example).

**Day in the life**: look for transitions, waiting, manual work, repetition, emotional strain. From it derive **comparable signals** (task frequency, who initiates, current alternative, waiting point, cost of error…).

**Pain scale**: 1 has a problem · 2 recognizes it · 3 searches for a solution · **4 built a workaround** · **5 has or seeks budget**. Levels 4–5 are useful early because actions and costs are visible.

**Screening**: **behaviour is stronger than a label**. Weak labels: aware, modern, busy, motivated. Observable signals: did X in the last month, paid for an alternative, built a manual process, delayed another task. A criterion that cannot be checked neutrally is weak for recruitment.

title.fr: Hypothèse de problème, priorisation et recrutement (Week 2)

fr: **Un problème n'est pas une feature manquante.** Non : « il n'y a pas de rappels automatiques ». Oui (mécanisme observable) : « après une échéance manquée, ils relancent le client à la main et ne peuvent pas prévoir leur trésorerie ».
**Anatomie** : **Segment** (qui) · **Context** (quand) · **Current path** (que se passe-t-il aujourd'hui) · **Barrier** (ce qui bloque) · **Consequence** (ce qui est perdu).
**5 types de coûts** : time, money, risk, emotion, social. Question clé : quelle conséquence change réellement le comportement ?

**Gabarit** : « We believe [segment], in [context], uses [current path], faces [barrier], which leads to [consequence]. » **Elle s'affaiblit si** des participants pertinents ne se rappellent pas d'épisode récent ou si la conséquence ne change pas le comportement.

**Signaux** : à l'appui = épisodes récents répétés, contournement existant, coût visible ; **disconfirming** = épisode rare, quelqu'un d'autre en est responsable, pas de conséquence, l'alternative marche bien. *Sans signal de réfutation, on collecte des compliments au lieu d'apprendre.*

**Persuasif ≠ testable** : « Les freelancers ont besoin d'un service pratique de contrôle des paiements » (faible) vs « les designers avec 3-8 clients relancent les paiements à la main, ça prend du temps et rend la trésorerie incertaine » (plus fort).
**Choisir le segment de départ pour apprendre**, pas pour séduire : accès, fréquence des épisodes, coût de l'inaction, homogénéité, observabilité (notes de 1 à 5). Le choix est **temporaire**.

**Recruter l'expérience, pas l'accord** : inclure (designer indépendant, émet ses factures, 3-8 clients actifs, retard de paiement dans les 60 jours, a personnellement relancé) ; exclure (salarié, quelqu'un d'autre gère les paiements, 100 % d'acompte, pas d'épisode récent, pas de communication client).
**Sorties Week 2 → Week 3** : segment, screener, respondents, interview guide. *Formative work, non noté.*
en: **A problem is not a missing feature.** Not: “There are no automated reminders”. Yes (observable mechanism): “After a missed due date, they message the client manually and cannot forecast cash flow”.
**Anatomy**: **Segment** (who) · **Context** (when) · **Current path** (what happens today) · **Barrier** (what blocks progress) · **Consequence** (what is lost).
**5 kinds of cost**: time, money, risk, emotion, social. Key question: which consequence actually changes behaviour?

**Template**: “We believe [segment], in [context], uses [current path], faces [barrier], which leads to [consequence].” **It weakens if** relevant participants cannot recall a recent episode or the consequence does not change behaviour.

**Signals**: supporting = recent episodes repeat, a workaround exists, the cost is visible; **disconfirming** = episode is rare, another person owns it, no consequence, alternative works well. *Without a disconfirming signal, a team collects compliments instead of learning.*

**Persuasive ≠ testable**: “Freelancers need a convenient payment-control service” (weak) vs “designers with 3–8 clients chase late payments manually; this takes time and makes cash flow uncertain” (stronger).
**Choose a starting segment for learning**, not presentation appeal: access, episode frequency, cost of inaction, homogeneity, observability (scored 1–5). The choice is **temporary**.

**Recruit for experience, not agreement**: include (self-employed designer, issues own invoices, 3–8 active clients, late payment in 60 days, personally chased); exclude (salaried, another person owns payments, 100% prepayment, no recent episode, no client communication).
**Week 2 output → Week 3**: segment, screener, respondents, interview guide. *Formative work, not graded.*

title.en: Problem interviews and the Mom Test (Week 3)

fr: **Un « oui » poli peut être une mauvaise donnée.** « Would you use an app that reminds you about every deadline? » → « Probably, yes » : ça sonne bien, ça ne prouve rien. Mieux : « Tell me about the last important deadline you had to track ».
**Règle de recherche** : une question doit laisser la place de **réfuter l'hypothèse** (le participant doit pouvoir dire « il n'y a pas de problème »).

**But** : comprendre le **mécanisme du problème** (quand ? que se passe-t-il aujourd'hui ? qu'est-ce qui gêne ? qu'en résulte-t-il ?). Ce n'est **ni de la vente ni du brainstorming** : on n'a pas à demander l'approbation de l'idée, une liste de features, une promesse d'achat, des conseils au fondateur.

**3 types d'interview** : **Problem** (le problème existe-t-il, comment fonctionne-t-il ?) · **Solution** (comprend-il la solution, l'aide-t-elle ?) · **Expert** (comment marchent le marché, le process, les contraintes ?). *La Week 3 ne traite que l'interview problème.*
**Force des réponses** (faible → forte) : « Great idea » · « This is usually difficult » · « Next time I would… » · « Last week this happened… » · « I spent 3 hours / paid / built a workaround ».
**4 signaux** : **Fact**, **Trigger**, **Action**, **Consequence**. Un insight naît de la **comparaison entre interviews**, pas d'une belle citation.
**Mom Test – 3 règles** : (1) parler de **leur vie**, pas de ton idée ; (2) demander le **passé**, pas le futur ; (3) **écouter plus que parler**.

**4 pièges** : (1) les **compliments** (« Do you like our idea? ») → « How do you currently track deadlines? » ; (2) les **intentions futures sont bon marché** (« Would you check the app daily? ») → « When did you last check? » ; (3) le **pitch** transforme l'échange en revue ; (4) la **demande de feature** cache le problème → « What would become easier? Tell me about a time when that mattered ».
**Suivre l'épisode** : When did this last happen ? What triggered it ? What did you do first ? What happened next ? How did it end ?
en: **A polite “yes” can be bad data.** “Would you use an app that reminds you about every deadline?” → “Probably, yes”: sounds nice, proves nothing. Better: “Tell me about the last important deadline you had to track”.
**Research rule**: a question must leave room to **disprove the hypothesis** (the participant must be able to say “there is no problem”).

**Goal**: understand the **problem mechanism** (when does it occur? what happens today? what gets in the way? what results?). It is **not sales or brainstorming**: don’t ask for approval of the idea, a feature wish list, a promise to buy, or advice to the founder.

**3 interview types**: **Problem** (does the problem exist and how does it work?) · **Solution** (does the person understand the solution and does it help?) · **Expert** (how do the market, process or constraints work?). *Week 3 focuses only on the problem interview.*
**Answer strength** (weak → strong): “Great idea” · “This is usually difficult” · “Next time I would…” · “Last week this happened…” · “I spent 3 hours / paid / built a workaround”.
**4 signals**: **Fact**, **Trigger**, **Action**, **Consequence**. An insight emerges after **comparing interviews**, not from one attractive quote.
**Mom Test – 3 rules**: (1) talk about **their life**, not your idea; (2) ask about the **past**, not the future; (3) **listen more than you talk**.

**4 traps**: (1) **compliments** (“Do you like our idea?”) → “How do you currently track deadlines?”; (2) **future intentions are cheap** (“Would you check the app daily?”) → “When did you last check?”; (3) a **pitch** turns the conversation into a review; (4) a **feature request** hides the problem → “What would become easier? Tell me about a time when that mattered”.
**Follow the episode**: When did this last happen? What triggered it? What did you do first? What happened next? How did it end?

title.fr: Construire le guide d'interview et le Task 1.1
title.en: Building the interview guide and Task 1.1

fr: **Commencer par 3 inconnues**, pas par des questions : « qu'est-ce qui doit être plus clair après la conversation ? » (ex. fréquence de la confusion, méthode actuelle de suivi, conséquences d'une échéance manquée). Si une question ne réduit pas une incertitude, on l'enlève.
**5 parties du guide** : 1 **Opening and consent** · 2 **Context** · 3 **Recent episode** · 4 **Actions and impact** · 5 **Closing**. C'est un itinéraire, pas un questionnaire rigide.

**Ouverture** (30 premières secondes) : neutre, ne nomme **pas** le produit, ne sous-entend pas que le problème est prouvé ; mentionne la durée (~20 min), l'accord pour prendre des notes, le droit de sauter une question.

**Contexte** : court échauffement (semaine type, types d'échéances, d'où vient l'info, comment on la suit). **Épisode récent** : « Tell me about your last deadline » – noter date, séquence, personnes, résultat. **Sonder la séquence** sans défendre l'hypothèse.
**Alternatives actuelles** : manual, paid, social, avoidance. **Conséquences** rendues observables : time, money, risk, emotion (« What happened because of that? »).
**Clôture** : What important question did I miss ? Puis-je te recontacter ? Qui d'autre ? Un document anonymisable ? **Ne jamais finir par « So, what do you think of our idea? »**
**Exemple de transcript** : deux sources de dates contradictoires (email vs WhatsApp) → pivot possible : le problème est la **confiance dans la source**, pas la mémoire ni les rappels.
**Pilote en triades** : Interviewer / Participant / Observer, interview de 8 min puis 3 min de feedback.

**Task 1.1 (evidence package)** – 8 parties : Revised Segment Portrait · Problem hypothesis · One disconfirming signal · Guide (10-12 core questions) · Criteria and short screener · Two completed interviews · Two anonymised records · Methodological self-check. **À rendre en un seul fichier avant le début de la Week 5.**

**Barème (100 pts)** : Segment Portrait + hypothesis **15** · Interview guide **25** · Respondent fit + ethical procedure **10** · Two anonymised interview records **30** · Analysis + methodological self-check **20**. Interviews réelles seulement **après la Week 4**. Pas encore : CJM, synthèse/codage, Problem Statements + Job Stories, prototype.
en: **Start with 3 unknowns**, not questions: “what must become clearer after the conversation?” (e.g. frequency of confusion, current tracking method, consequences of a missed deadline). If a question does not reduce an uncertainty, remove it.
**5 parts of the guide**: 1 **Opening and consent** · 2 **Context** · 3 **Recent episode** · 4 **Actions and impact** · 5 **Closing**. It is a route, not a rigid questionnaire.
**Opening** (first 30 seconds): neutral, **do not** name the product or imply the problem is proven; mention duration (~20 min), permission to take notes, right to skip questions.

**Context**: short warm-up (typical week, kinds of deadlines, where info comes from, how it is tracked). **Recent episode**: “Tell me about your last deadline” – capture date, sequence, people, outcome. **Probe the sequence** without defending the hypothesis.
**Current alternatives**: manual, paid, social, avoidance. **Consequences** made observable: time, money, risk, emotion (“What happened because of that?”).
**Closing**: What important question did I miss? May I follow up? Who else should I speak with? Any document that could be anonymized? **Never finish with “So, what do you think of our idea?”**
**Transcript example**: two conflicting date sources (email vs WhatsApp) → possible pivot: the problem is **source trust**, not memory or reminders.
**Pilot in triads**: Interviewer / Participant / Observer, 8-minute interview then 3-minute feedback.

**Task 1.1 (evidence package)** – 8 parts: Revised Segment Portrait · Problem hypothesis · One disconfirming signal · Guide (10–12 core questions) · Criteria and short screener · Two completed interviews · Two anonymised records · Methodological self-check. **Submit as one file before Week 5 begins.**

**Grading (100 pts)**: Segment Portrait + hypothesis **15** · Interview guide **25** · Respondent fit + ethical procedure **10** · Two anonymised interview records **30** · Analysis + methodological self-check **20**. Real interviews only **after Week 4**. Not yet: CJM, coding/synthesis board, Problem Statements + Job Stories, prototype.

title.fr: Analyser les interviews : preuves, codes, thèmes, insights (Week 5)
title.en: Analysing interviews: evidence, codes, themes, insights (Week 5)

fr: **Chaîne d'analyse** : Raw data → **Evidence** (qu'a dit/fait le client ?) → **Codes** (de quoi parle ce fragment ?) → **Themes** (quels codes vont ensemble ?) → **Patterns** (ce qui se répète, se relie ou se contredit) → **Insights** (que signifie le motif ?) → **Customer journey** (où ça se passe ?) → **Learning** (ce qui change dans notre compréhension).
**Pourquoi analyser** : éviter de se fier aux citations marquantes, réduire le biais de confirmation, comparer les clients systématiquement, distinguer preuve et interprétation, trouver l'inattendu.

**Bonne preuve** : spécifique, liée à une situation réelle, traçable jusqu'à l'interview, basée sur ce que le client a vécu. **Comportement réel > hypothétique** (« I stopped using the service after it arrived two hours late » > « I would probably stop… »).

**Coding** = attribuer une **étiquette courte** à un fragment significatif. Bon code : court, spécifique, significatif, relié à la preuve, réutilisable. À éviter : Problem, Customer, App, Bad experience. À préférer : Price sensitivity, Lack of trust, Time pressure, Need for predictability, Competing priorities.

**Inductive coding** : DATA → CODE → THEME. Ne pas forcer les données dans l'hypothèse de départ. **Code** = étiquette spécifique ; **Theme** = concept plus large qui relie des codes (ex. TIME & CONVENIENCE).

**Patterns** : répétition, comportements similaires, séquences, déclencheurs et conséquences, contradictions. **La fréquence n'est pas tout** : intensité, conséquences comportementales, pertinence, contexte, cohérence. Un comportement très conséquent peut compter plus que plusieurs remarques légères.

**Insight** = interprétation fondée sur des preuves qui explique un comportement/une motivation/une expérience. **Insight ≠ solution** (« Customers struggle to maintain usage when their routine changes » = insight ; « We should add reminders » = solution). Structure : « Customers [behaviour] when [context], which suggests [interpretation] ».

**Démo food delivery** : « I see the delivery fee and decide not to order » → evidence *delivery fee affects decision* → code **Price sensitivity** → thème **Cost**. Tension : commodité (« no time to cook ») **mais** coût/incertitude/confiance (« I don't trust the estimated delivery time »).
**Revisiter l'hypothèse** : Supported / Partially supported / Challenged / Inconclusive. On ne la change **que si les preuves le suggèrent**, pas parce qu'elle « sonne mieux ».

**Current-State Customer Journey Map** : ce que les clients vivent **maintenant** (pas l'état futur idéal). Étapes possibles : Need → Discovery → Consideration → Adoption → Use → Friction → Drop-off / Continued use ; pour chaque étape : action, touchpoint, thought, emotion, pain point, evidence.

**Principe** : *evidence before interpretation, interpretation before solution.* Exit ticket : pattern le plus important, preuve, prochaine question. Réflexion : WE THOUGHT… / WE LEARNED… / WE NEED TO TEST…
en: **Analysis chain**: Raw data → **Evidence** (what did the customer say/do?) → **Codes** (what is this fragment about?) → **Themes** (which codes belong together?) → **Patterns** (what repeats, connects or contradicts?) → **Insights** (what does the pattern mean?) → **Customer journey** (where does it happen?) → **Learning** (what changes in our understanding).
**Why analyse**: avoid relying on memorable quotes, reduce confirmation bias, compare customers systematically, distinguish evidence from interpretation, discover the unexpected.

**Good evidence**: specific, connected to a real situation, traceable to the interview, based on what the customer actually experienced. **Real behaviour > hypotheticals** (“I stopped using the service after it arrived two hours late” > “I would probably stop…”).

**Coding** = assigning a **short label** to a meaningful fragment. Good code: short, specific, meaningful, connected to the evidence, reusable across interviews. Avoid: Problem, Customer, App, Bad experience. Prefer: Price sensitivity, Lack of trust, Time pressure, Need for predictability, Competing priorities.
**Inductive coding**: DATA → CODE → THEME. Don’t force data to fit your original hypothesis. **Code** = specific label; **Theme** = broader concept connecting related codes (e.g. TIME & CONVENIENCE).

**Patterns**: repetition, similar behaviour, sequences, triggers and consequences, contradictions. **Frequency is not everything**: intensity, behavioural consequences, relevance, context, consistency. One highly consequential behaviour may matter more than several casual comments.

**Insight** = evidence-based interpretation that explains customer behaviour, motivation or experience. **Insight ≠ solution** (“Customers struggle to maintain usage when their routine changes” = insight; “We should add reminders” = solution). Structure: “Customers [behaviour] when [context], which suggests [interpretation]”.

**Food delivery demo**: “I see the delivery fee and decide not to order” → evidence *delivery fee affects decision* → code **Price sensitivity** → theme **Cost**. Tension: convenience (“no time to cook”) **but** cost/uncertainty/trust (“I don’t trust the estimated delivery time”).
**Revisit the hypothesis**: Supported / Partially supported / Challenged / Inconclusive. Change it **only because the evidence suggests it**, not because it “sounds better”.

**Current-State Customer Journey Map**: what customers experience **now** (not the ideal future). Possible stages: Need → Discovery → Consideration → Adoption → Use → Friction → Drop-off / Continued use; for each stage: action, touchpoint, thought, emotion, pain point, evidence.

**Principle**: *evidence before interpretation, interpretation before solution.* Exit ticket: most important pattern, its evidence, next question. Reflection: WE THOUGHT… / WE LEARNED… / WE NEED TO TEST…

qcm.q: According to Lesson 1, what is the hidden risk for a team?
qcm.correct: Confident execution of the wrong idea
wrong: Executing too slowly against the plan
Spending too little on marketing
Hiring the wrong technical staff
qcm.why: Une équipe peut livrer à l'heure et dans le budget et quand même échouer si le problème client n'a jamais été réel : c'est l'exécution confiante de la mauvaise idée.

qcm.q: How is Customer Development defined in the course?
qcm.correct: Turning assumptions into evidence, and evidence into decisions
wrong: A method to sell a finished product to as many buyers as possible
A survey technique to describe average market trends and attitudes
A process to build product features as fast as possible
qcm.why: Assumption → Evidence → Decision. Ce n'est ni de la vente, ni une étude de marché descriptive, ni un process de build.

qcm.q: Which stage of the Customer Development model does this course concentrate on?
qcm.correct: Stage 1: Customer Discovery
wrong: Stage 2: Customer Validation
Stage 3: Customer Creation
Stage 4: Company Building
qcm.why: Ordre : Discovery (problème réel ?), Validation (le modèle se répète ?), Creation (la demande peut croître ?), Company Building (l'organisation passe à l'échelle ?). Le cours se concentre sur l'étape 1.

qcm.q: In a startup that is 'searching' for a model, what counts as progress?
qcm.correct: Reduced uncertainty
wrong: Reliable delivery
Accurate forecasts
Lower production costs
qcm.why: Search : hypothèses provisoires, l'apprentissage change le plan, progrès = incertitude réduite. Execution : progrès = livraison fiable.

qcm.q: What are the four questions Customer Discovery answers before a team commits to a solution?
qcm.correct: Who, What, How now, How sure
wrong: Who, Where, How much, How fast
What, Why, When, How many
Who, What, Price, Profit
qcm.why: WHO (quelles personnes), WHAT (quel problème), HOW NOW (alternatives actuelles), HOW SURE (preuves pour ou contre).

qcm.q: What is the 'planning trap'?
qcm.correct: A business plan writes assumptions as if they were facts
wrong: A plan that is updated too often to be useful to the team
A plan that lists too many financial forecasts for investors
A plan that is only written after the product has launched
qcm.why: Le plan cache l'incertitude. Discovery réécrit chaque phrase du plan en affirmation testable.

qcm.q: Which statement is true about running Product and Customer tracks?
qcm.correct: A product milestone is not evidence that the customer hypothesis is true
wrong: Launching the product proves that the customer problem exists
Customer work should only start once the product has launched
The two tracks must never be run in parallel by the same team
qcm.why: Les deux pistes tournent en parallèle et un jalon produit (build, launch) ne valide pas l'hypothèse client.

qcm.q: Which is a risk listed under 'Problem risk'?
qcm.correct: The problem is weak, rare or tolerated
wrong: We chose the wrong segment
The market is too small to attract investors
The team lacks technical skills
qcm.why: Customer risk = mauvais segment ; Problem risk = problème faible, rare ou toléré ; Value risk = trop petit pour motiver l'action.

qcm.q: What are the four possible outcomes at the decision gate?
qcm.correct: Continue, narrow, pivot or stop
wrong: Scale, hire, launch or fundraise
Continue, expand, invest or wait
Test, survey, sell or exit
qcm.why: Une boucle utile se termine par une décision changée : continuer, resserrer, pivoter ou arrêter.

qcm.q: What is the typical failure mode of 'Selling' compared with Customer Discovery?
qcm.correct: Agreement is mistaken for evidence
wrong: Pitching the idea instead of listening
Broad averages hide the context
Too many stories and no numbers
qcm.why: Selling : l'accord est pris pour une preuve. Discovery : pitcher l'idée. Market research : les moyennes larges cachent le contexte.

qcm.q: 'She opened three banking apps and copied balances into Notes.' What is this statement?
qcm.correct: An observation
wrong: An interpretation
A claim
A hypothesis
qcm.why: C'est ce qu'on a directement vu. « Elle veut une vue unique de son argent » = interprétation ; « les étudiants ont besoin d'un système de budget consolidé » = claim.

qcm.q: Which term means 'a specific, testable claim'?
qcm.correct: Hypothesis
wrong: Assumption
Insight
Decision
qcm.why: Assumption = croyance traitée comme incertaine ; Insight = interprétation qui explique un motif ; Decision = changement d'action justifié par des preuves.

qcm.q: Which are the four parts of a customer problem in Lesson 1?
qcm.correct: Segment, context, friction, consequence
wrong: Segment, product, price, distribution channel
Customer, competitor, feature list, cost structure
Context, proposed solution, friction, revenue model
qcm.why: Segment (qui), Context (quand/où), Friction (ce qui bloque), Consequence (coût, retard, risque, émotion). Si une partie est floue, l'hypothèse est difficile à tester.

qcm.q: A student says 'I want one app that shows all my accounts.' How should you treat it?
qcm.correct: As a solution request; ask for the story behind it
wrong: As validated proof that the problem is real and urgent
As a feature request to add straight to the roadmap
As a good reason to stop the interview and thank them
qcm.why: « I want an app » est une demande de solution. On demande : qu'est-il arrivé la dernière fois, qu'as-tu fait, qu'est-ce qui était difficile, qu'est-ce que ça a coûté ?

qcm.q: Which test checks whether a problem hypothesis is neutral?
qcm.correct: Remove every solution word and see if it is still true
wrong: Count how many of the interviewed people agree with it
Check that it names the product that is planned to be built
Make sure it contains a clear price estimate for the solution
qcm.why: Si l'énoncé ne tient plus sans mots de solution, ce n'est pas une hypothèse de problème.

qcm.q: On the evidence ladder, which is the STRONGEST type of evidence?
qcm.correct: Repeated behaviour with real cost or commitment
wrong: A recent specific story with observable detail and dates
A current workaround or alternative the customer uses
A general attitude or preference expressed in words
qcm.why: Échelle : 5 comportement répété avec coût/engagement > 4 histoire récente > 3 contournement > 2 attitude > 1 intention future.

qcm.q: Which question is the stronger interview question?
qcm.correct: Tell me about the last time this happened
wrong: Would you use a tool that fixed this problem for you?
Would you pay for a solution to this problem?
Do you like the idea of a product that solves this?
qcm.why: Le passé est ancré dans des preuves existantes. Les questions au conditionnel invitent à la politesse, à l'imagination et à la prédiction.

qcm.q: Problem intensity is best shown by which combination?
qcm.correct: Frequency, consequence and current cost
wrong: Complaint volume and how loud the tone is
Number of interviews completed and quotes gathered
Feature requests and satisfaction ratings received
qcm.why: Intensité ≠ volume de plaintes : une plainte bruyante peut avoir peu de conséquences, un contournement silencieux peut coûter des heures chaque semaine.

qcm.q: Why should contradictions and negative cases be recorded?
qcm.correct: They protect the team from confirmation bias
wrong: They show that the interview was badly run by the team
They should be ignored as one-off outliers in the data
They prove that the hypothesis is definitely correct
qcm.why: Les contradictions sont des données. On range les preuves en Supports, Challenges, Unknown.

qcm.q: Which is NOT one of the four qualities of decision-ready evidence?
qcm.correct: Unanimous
wrong: Relevant
Traceable
Ethical
qcm.why: Les quatre qualités : relevant, varied, traceable, ethical. L'unanimité n'est pas exigée (on cherche aussi des cas qui contredisent).

qcm.q: What is the difference between a target audience and a research segment?
qcm.correct: A segment is one screenable situation with comparable experience
wrong: A segment is always a much bigger group than the audience
An audience is defined by behaviour, while a segment is defined by age
There is no difference between them; the terms are synonyms
qcm.why: L'audience est un marché large (utile pour le dimensionner) ; le segment est une situation pertinente, un comportement observable, des contraintes comparables, filtrables avant l'interview.

qcm.q: Which are the four lenses that turn a category into a research segment?
qcm.correct: Context, behavior, constraint, consequence
wrong: Age, income, city, education level
Product, price, place, promotion strategy
Need, budget, authority, timing of purchase
qcm.why: Context (quand ?), Behavior (que se passe-t-il aujourd'hui ?), Constraint (qu'est-ce qui bloque ?), Consequence (qu'est-ce qui est perdu ?).

qcm.q: Which option defines the best research segment?
qcm.correct: Year 2–3 students who applied for an internship in the last 60 days and rewrote their CV
wrong: Students who need a career service and are looking for help with their professional future
Ambitious young people aged 18–24 who care about their career and want to get ahead in life
Modern, digital-native students who are interested in what happens after university ends
qcm.why: L'option B du cours contient une expérience récente, une action et une limite de temps. Les autres sont des étiquettes vagues.

qcm.q: Which customer role controls the budget?
qcm.correct: Economic buyer
wrong: Decision maker
Recommender
Saboteur
qcm.why: Economic buyer = contrôle le budget ; Decision maker = donne le oui final ; Recommender = peut faire avancer ou stopper ; Saboteur = protège le statu quo.

qcm.q: On the pain scale, which levels are especially useful early because actions and costs are visible?
qcm.correct: Levels 4–5 (built a workaround; has or seeks budget)
wrong: Levels 1–2 (has a problem; recognizes that it exists)
Level 3 only (searches for a solution but has not acted yet)
Levels 1 and 5 only (has a problem, or has budget)
qcm.why: Un contournement ou un budget rendent actions, coûts et contraintes observables.

qcm.q: Which is a weak screening criterion (a label rather than an observable signal)?
qcm.correct: Motivated
wrong: Paid for an alternative
Built a manual process
Did X in the last month
qcm.why: Aware, modern, busy, motivated sont faibles : on ne peut pas les vérifier neutralement. Les signaux observables sont des comportements passés.

qcm.q: Which is an observable problem mechanism (not just a missing feature)?
qcm.correct: After a missed due date, they message the client manually and cannot forecast cash flow
wrong: There are no automated reminders for the people who send invoices to their clients
They need a convenient payment-control service that is modern and easy to use every day
The current invoicing tools look old and are not attractive to modern freelancers
qcm.why: Un problème n'est pas une feature manquante : on décrit ce qui se passe aujourd'hui et ses conséquences.

qcm.q: Which is a disconfirming signal for a problem hypothesis?
qcm.correct: The episode is rare, or another person owns the problem
wrong: Recent episodes repeat across several different participants
A workaround exists and clearly costs the person time
The cost of the problem is visible in their behaviour
qcm.why: Les trois autres options soutiennent l'hypothèse. Réfutent : épisode rare, quelqu'un d'autre en est responsable, pas de conséquence, alternative qui marche bien.

qcm.q: What is the template for a strong problem hypothesis in Week 2?
qcm.correct: We believe [segment], in [context], uses [current path], faces [barrier], which leads to [consequence]
wrong: We believe [product] will help [segment] save [time] at [price] compared with the alternatives they use
We believe [feature] is needed by [market] because [competitor lacks it] and users keep asking for it
We believe [segment] will buy [solution] when [promotion runs] and the price feels right to them
qcm.why: Le gabarit contient segment, contexte, current path, barrier et consequence, et aucun mot de solution.

qcm.q: How should you choose the first segment to study?
qcm.correct: For learning: access, frequency, cost of inaction, homogeneity, observability
wrong: For presentation appeal: the biggest and most impressive market on the slide
For agreement: the people who like the idea the most and say yes quickly
For convenience: friends who will happily say yes and respond fast to messages
qcm.why: Le choix est temporaire et sert à apprendre, pas à séduire. Critères notés de 1 à 5 : access, episode frequency, cost of inaction, homogeneity, observability.

qcm.q: In the late-payment case, which respondent should be EXCLUDED from recruitment?
qcm.correct: A designer who always takes 100% prepayment
wrong: A designer with 5 active clients and self-issued invoices
A designer who personally chased a client for payment
A designer with a late payment in the last month
qcm.why: Recruter l'expérience, pas l'accord : qui prend 100 % d'acompte n'a pas vécu l'épisode de retard de paiement. Les autres correspondent aux critères d'inclusion.

qcm.q: Which is one of the three Mom Test rules?
qcm.correct: Ask about the past, not the future
wrong: Describe your idea before asking questions
Ask what features they would want
Talk more so the person feels comfortable
qcm.why: Les 3 règles : parler de leur vie (pas de ton idée), demander le passé (pas le futur), écouter plus que parler.

qcm.q: Which of these is a leading (dangerous) question?
qcm.correct: You receive announcements in several chats, don't you?
wrong: How did you learn about it?
What did you do when you could not find the information?
What happened because of the delay?
qcm.why: Elle suggère la réponse attendue et la donne comme un fait. Une bonne question laisse le participant dire « il n'y a pas de problème ».

qcm.q: Why is 'Would you check the app every day?' a weak question?
qcm.correct: Intention is a hypothesis; past behaviour is evidence
wrong: It is too expensive and time-consuming to ask in a real interview
It is a sales question about the price of the planned product
It asks about too many different problems at the same time
qcm.why: Mieux : « When did you last check your deadlines? What exactly did you do? »

qcm.q: Which interview type does Week 3 focus on?
qcm.correct: The problem interview
wrong: The solution interview
The expert interview
The sales interview
qcm.why: Trois types : problème (le problème existe-t-il ?), solution (aide-t-elle ?), expert (comment marche le marché ?). Week 3 = problème uniquement.

qcm.q: Which answer is the STRONGEST evidence in a problem interview?
qcm.correct: "I spent 3 hours on it and built a workaround"
wrong: "This is usually difficult for people like me"
"Great idea, I think it will really help"
"Next time I would probably try that out"
qcm.why: Temps dépensé, argent payé ou contournement construit = comportement réel. « Great idea » est la plus faible.

qcm.q: In the transcript excerpt (email date vs WhatsApp date), what possible pivot is suggested?
qcm.correct: The problem may be source trust, not memory or reminders
wrong: The problem is that students simply forget their deadlines
The solution should clearly be a new reminders app
There is no real problem here that needs to be solved
qcm.why: Le participant ne savait pas quelle source était officielle. Un seul épisode peut changer la définition du problème.

qcm.q: Which are the five parts of the interview guide?
qcm.correct: Opening and consent, context, recent episode, actions and impact, closing
wrong: Pitch, demo, feedback, pricing and a closing thank-you note
Introduction, features list, ranking, budget question, thanks
Context, proposed solution, objections, pricing, contract signing
qcm.why: C'est un itinéraire, pas un questionnaire rigide. L'épisode récent est le cœur de l'interview.

qcm.q: How should the interview opening treat the product?
qcm.correct: It should not name the product or imply the problem is proven
wrong: It should present the product first to build interest
It should promise a discount as a reward for taking part
It should describe the planned solution in some detail
qcm.why: Une ouverture neutre réduit l'envie de faire plaisir. On précise la durée, la prise de notes et le droit de sauter une question.

qcm.q: Which way of closing the interview is recommended?
qcm.correct: Ask what important question you missed and who else to speak with
wrong: Ask what they think of your idea and whether they like it
Ask them to promise they will buy the product later
Thank them and end the call without any follow-up plan
qcm.why: Clôture : question manquée, recontact, autres personnes, document anonymisable. Ne jamais finir par « So, what do you think of our idea? »

qcm.q: In the Task 1.1 grading, which part is worth the MOST points?
qcm.correct: Two anonymised interview records (30 points)
wrong: Problem-interview guide (25 points)
Analysis and methodological self-check (20 points)
Segment Portrait and hypothesis (15 points)
qcm.why: Barème sur 100 : records 30 ; guide 25 ; analyse + self-check 20 ; portrait + hypothèse 15 ; respondent fit + éthique 10.

qcm.q: When are the real interviews for Task 1.1 conducted and the package submitted?
qcm.correct: Interviews after Week 4; submission before Week 5 begins
wrong: Interviews in Week 3; submission after the end of Week 5
Interviews in Week 2; submission during the Week 3 class
Interviews after Week 5; submission at the end of the term
qcm.why: Week 3 = guide + pilote. Interviews réelles seulement après la Week 4. Rendu en un seul fichier avant le début de la Week 5.

qcm.q: What is the correct order of the analytical process in Week 5?
qcm.correct: Evidence → Codes → Themes → Patterns → Insights
wrong: Themes → Evidence → Codes → Insights → Patterns
Codes → Themes → Evidence → Patterns → Insights
Insights → Patterns → Themes → Codes → Evidence
qcm.why: On part des données brutes, on extrait la preuve, on code, on regroupe en thèmes, on cherche les patterns, puis on formule des insights.

qcm.q: What is the difference between a code and a theme?
qcm.correct: A code is a specific label; a theme groups related codes
wrong: A code is a broad concept; a theme is a specific label
They are two different names for exactly the same thing
A theme is a direct quote; a code is an interpretation
qcm.why: Codes = briques de construction (Time pressure, Price sensitivity). Thème = concept plus large qui les relie (TIME & CONVENIENCE).

qcm.q: Which is a good code according to the course?
qcm.correct: Need for predictability
wrong: Problem with the service
Bad experience overall
Customer feedback
qcm.why: Un bon code est court, spécifique, significatif et réutilisable. « Problem », « Customer », « App », « Bad experience » sont trop vagues.

qcm.q: What does inductive coding mean?
qcm.correct: Let categories emerge from the data instead of forcing your hypothesis
wrong: Start from the hypothesis and look for confirming quotes only
Copy the customer's own words as codes without interpreting
Code only the most frequently mentioned comments in each interview
qcm.why: DATA → CODE → THEME. On laisse les catégories émerger de ce que les clients ont dit et fait.

qcm.q: Which is an insight rather than a solution?
qcm.correct: Customers struggle to maintain usage when their routine changes
wrong: We should add reminders and push notifications to the product
We should lower the delivery fee for all student customers
We should build a loyalty program to keep users engaged
qcm.why: Insight ≠ solution. L'insight explique un motif ; la solution (« add reminders ») vient seulement après : evidence → pattern → insight → what to test next.

qcm.q: Why is frequency 'not everything' when identifying patterns?
qcm.correct: One highly consequential behaviour can matter more than several casual comments
wrong: Only the most frequent statement is ever relevant to the analysis, whatever its context
Frequency can never be used at all when analysing interview data of any kind
Casual comments are always more reliable than a single consequential behaviour
qcm.why: Il faut aussi regarder l'intensité, les conséquences comportementales, le contexte, la cohérence.

qcm.q: In the food-delivery demo, what code fits 'I see the delivery fee and decide not to order'?
qcm.correct: Price sensitivity
wrong: Need for predictability
Preference for familiarity
Lack of time
qcm.why: Preuve : le tarif de livraison influence la décision → code Price sensitivity → thème Cost.

qcm.q: What must a Current-State Customer Journey Map describe?
qcm.correct: What customers experience now, based on interview evidence
wrong: The ideal future experience customers will have with our product
The company's internal sales process from lead to signed deal
The list of features that are planned for the next release
qcm.why: État actuel, pas futur idéal. Étapes possibles : Need → Discovery → Consideration → Adoption → Use → Friction → Drop-off / Continued use.

qcm.q: After analysis, which is NOT a valid status for the original hypothesis?
qcm.correct: Proven with certainty
wrong: Partially supported
Challenged
Inconclusive / needs more research
qcm.why: Statuts : Supported, Partially supported, Challenged, Inconclusive. On ne prouve jamais avec certitude, et on ne change pas l'hypothèse parce qu'elle « sonne mieux ».
